summary: Route leaks in BGP have caused frequent significant disruptions, but there has been no common definition of the term. This informational RFC offers a working definition and classifies the kinds of route leaks seen in real incidents.

eli5.summary: Sometimes a network wrongly announces routes it should keep to itself, sending traffic the wrong way. This defines what that means.

questions: what is a bgp route leak
subtitle: When routing announcements escape their intended boundaries

tldr.problem: BGP route leaks are announcements that propagate beyond their intended scope, misdirecting traffic through incorrect paths, causing frequent outages and disruptions.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines route leaks as violations of intended routing policies between autonomous systems and classifies them into six types based on real-world incidents, from accidental misconfigurations to unauthorized multi-hop propagation.
tldr.outcome: This working definition and taxonomy help the network operations community understand and work toward solutions for a systemic BGP vulnerability that has caused significant Internet disruptions.

today: RFC 7908 remains an Informational RFC that is not obsoleted. It serves as the foundational definition of route leaks and continues to guide work on detection and prevention mechanisms in the network operations community.

sections.title: The Route Leak Problem
sections.content:
BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is how the Internet's autonomous systems announce which network addresses they control and how to reach them. The basic problem is: route leaks are announcements that go beyond where they should. A network operator might accidentally announce a route to peers or upstream providers when policy says it should only stay within the organization.

These leaks happen frequently and cause real damage. Traffic destined for one network gets sent through the wrong path, which can result in eavesdropping, slow service, or complete outages. Before this RFC, there was no agreed-upon definition of what a route leak actually is, making it difficult to develop detection and prevention solutions.
sections.eli5: Internet traffic follows road signs that networks put up. Sometimes a network accidentally puts up wrong signs that send traffic the wrong way, breaking service.

sections.title: Defining Route Leaks
sections.content:
The RFC proposes this working definition: A route leak is the propagation of routing announcement(s) beyond their intended scope. That is, an AS announces a BGP route to another AS in violation of the intended policies of the receiver, the sender, or one of the ASes in the path.

The intended scope is usually defined by business relationships between ASes. Common relationships are customer (buys transit from), transit provider (sells transit to), and peer (exchanges traffic at equal cost). Routing policies differ based on these relationships. For example, when an AS learns a route from a transit provider, policy typically says not to announce it to peers or other transit providers.

Route leaks are usually accidental, caused by misconfiguration. However, they can sometimes be malicious. The result is traffic misdirection through unintended paths, which may cause eavesdropping, analysis, overload, or black holing.
sections.eli5: You learned about a shortcut from one friend. The rule is to only tell your friends you told about it to, but you accidentally told someone else. Now everyone uses it and things get messy.

sections.title: Classification of Route Leak Types
sections.content:
The RFC identifies six types of route leaks observed in real incidents:

Type 1: Hairpin Turn occurs when a multihomed customer learns a route from one upstream ISP and simply propagates it to another upstream ISP, without changing the prefix or AS path. The route makes a U-turn at the customer. Example: the 2012 Dodo-Telstra incident where 179,000 prefixes were leaked and accepted because the receiving ISP preferred customer announcements over peer announcements of the same prefix.

Type 2: Lateral ISP-ISP-ISP Leak happens between three sequential peering ISPs. ISP-B receives a route from ISP-A and leaks it to ISP-C. The policy between lateral peers is typically to only propagate customer prefixes, not peer prefixes.

Type 3: Transit-Provider Leak to Peer occurs when an AS leaks routes learned from its transit provider to a lateral peer, violating the expectation that only customer prefixes are shared with peers.

Type 4: Peer Prefix Leak to Transit Provider occurs when an AS leaks routes learned from a peer to its own transit provider. Examples include the 2015 Hathway-Airtel leak of Google prefixes causing service outages across Europe and Asia.

Type 5: Prefix Re-origination occurs when an AS re-announces a prefix as if originating it, stripping the received AS path. Sometimes a reverse path exists and data reaches the legitimate destination. Example: the 2010 China Telecom incident that hijacked prefixes globally for 18 minutes.

Type 6: Internal Prefix Leak occurs when an AS leaks internal prefixes and more-specific prefixes to transit providers or peers. These are typically short-lived but can momentarily redirect traffic over incorrect paths. In 2014, AS701 and AS705 leaked about 22,000 more-specific prefixes.
sections.eli5: Type 1: You pass the shortcut to another friend when you shouldn't. Type 2: A middle friend passes it along. Type 3-4: You tell the wrong type of friend. Type 5: You claim you invented the shortcut. Type 6: You accidentally leak your private routes.

sections.title: Understanding the Classification
sections.content:
The six types form a taxonomy that covers observed incidents, though the list is not exhaustive. Types 1 through 4 are similar in that they involve policy violations between different AS relationship contexts. Type 5 is notable because it can occur with various relationship contexts and scenarios.

The key insight is that many route leaks occur simply because a receiving AS fails to filter announcements properly. The RFC notes that solutions might involve better filtering policies, authentication of announcements, or detection mechanisms that identify anomalies in BGP paths.
sections.eli5: Most problems are about who says what to whom. Some problems are about fake origins. Better checking at each step would catch most of these.
